claims.text: Untreated, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native Fe-oxide film on its surface.
Increasing the exposure temperature from approximately 25°C to 60°C destabilizes the native oxide layer on Q235 steel in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
Temperature-induced destabilization of the native oxide accelerates corrosion initiation on Q235 steel.
Elevated temperature enhances dissolution of the passive oxide layer in the presence of chloride ions.
Elevated temperature increases defect formation within the passive oxide layer in the presence of chloride ions.
Oxide dissolution and defect formation reduce the protective capacity of the surface film.
Loss of oxide-film protective capacity promotes local film breakdown and corrosion initiation.
At approximately 25°C, the native oxide film on Q235 steel in 3.5 wt% NaCl remains relatively intact.
Untreated Q235 steel in 3.5 wt% NaCl has a lower corrosion rate at approximately 25°C than at 60°C.
Q235 steel tested at 60°C will exhibit lower polarization resistance than Q235 steel tested at 25°C.
Q235 steel tested at 60°C will exhibit higher corrosion current density than Q235 steel tested at 25°C.
Electrochemical impedance spectra will indicate greater corrosion-related degradation at 60°C than at 25°C.
SEM will reveal more localized corrosion, pitting, or oxide breakdown after exposure at 60°C than after exposure at 25°C.
Potentiodynamic polarization can provide corrosion current density and polarization resistance measurements for corrosion assessment in saline electrolyte.
OCP stabilization, EIS, potentiodynamic polarization, and post-exposure SEM can be combined in an electrochemical corrosion study.
SEM can specifically determine native-oxide integrity and detect pitting or oxide breakdown in this Q235 experiment.
Pretreatments or additional aggressive species may alter the initial oxide composition and change the proposed temperature response.
Additional corrosion mechanisms may emerge outside the tested temperature range of approximately 25°C to 60°C.
A lack of statistically significant electrochemical and surface-degradation differences between 25°C and 60°C would falsify the proposed temperature effect.
